item.title: Better healthcare for a better nation. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B

The government’s plan to launch door‑to‑door healthcare services is exactly the kind of proactive, people‑centred initiative Bangladesh needs. For too long, access to healthcare has depended on geography, income, and the ability to navigate overcrowded facilities. Taking essential services directly to citizens - especially the elderly, the poor, and those living with chronic illnesses - is a meaningful step toward equity. This initiative recognizes a simple truth: Many Bangladeshis do not seek care because they cannot reach it. Distance, transport costs, long queues, and lost wages keep people away from clinics until their conditions worsen. A system that waits for patients to come forward is a system that leaves many behind. As such, by sending trained health workers into communities, the government is shifting from reactive care to preventive care - and that shift will save lives. The plan also aligns with Bangladesh’s broader public‑health needs. Non-communicable diseases are rising, and early detection of diabetes, hypertension, respiratory illnesses, and nutritional deficiencies can dramatically reduce long‑term costs and suffering. Door‑to‑door services can therefore bridge these gaps, offering screening, counselling, and referrals before problems escalate. However, such an initiative only succeeds when it is implemented properly. While Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain spoke of a nationwide program, we hope that it is being piloted properly. Such a program will also be hollow if it fails to reach rural areas, urban slums, and marginalized communities. It is also evident that Bangladesh needs more initiatives with this level of ambition and outreach. In addition, for healthcare in particular, such a project, while highly commendable, cannot replace community‑based healthcare needing expansion or local clinics strengthened. Door‑to‑door healthcare can become a cornerstone of a more inclusive, resilient health system for our country, but only if it is scaled, funded, and sustained with seriousness.

item.title: How to solve groundwater depletion. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B

Bangladesh’s geography includes the extensive river deltas formed by major rivers like the Ganges and Brahmaputra, alongside a network of hundreds of small rivers. The monsoon season, occurring from June to September, contributes to 70-80% of the annual rainfall, while the dry winter months last from December to February. The annual rainfall distribution varies regionally, with the west receiving around 1,500 mm and the northeast and southeast receiving about 3,000 mm. Despite being a country with numerous waterways and adequate rainfall, Bangladesh, unusually, faces severe water-related problems in different parts of the country due to low natural recharge and high water demand. The use of surface water has been in decline due to groundwater depletion and dependence on groundwater on the rise. The problem of managing groundwater in the drought-prone northwestern Barind tract is severe, where rainfall is low. Currently, groundwater is vital for life and livelihoods, serving as the main source of clean drinking water and supporting agriculture. Approximately 90% of groundwater withdrawal is for agricultural use. In densely populated regions, the demand for groundwater often exceeds the natural recharge rates, leading to a continual decline in water levels, a situation referred to as depletion. This brings significant challenges, including dry wells, increased pumping costs, and reduced water availability for urban areas and agriculture. The situation intensifies food insecurity and water shortages, particularly as climate change results in more frequent droughts and altered rainfall patterns. Against this backdrop, addressing groundwater depletion is critical. One strategy for mitigation involves using groundwater within safe yield limits, while another approach includes the artificial replenishment of groundwater aquifers. In the Barind region, the Barind Integrated Area Development Project officially started in 1985 under the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation. It was created to revitalize the impoverished by combating severe seasonal droughts, severe water scarcity, and the need for food security. The project was reconstituted and upgraded into the Barind Multipurpose Development Authority in 1992. Groundwater issues were not mitigated and attention was given to the surface water bodies. However, groundwater problems need to be mitigated since 78% of BMDA projects rely on groundwater. Coastal regions of Bangladesh suffer from severe salinity intrusion, exacerbated by sea-level rise and reduced river flow, rendering water unfit for consumption and agriculture, alongside arsenic and bacterial contamination, leading to health crises. The managed aquifer recharge (MAR) technique is proposed as a practical solution to these groundwater issues across various regions of Bangladesh. MAR is a strategic approach aimed at intentionally replenishing aquifers with water for subsequent retrieval or enhancement of environmental conditions. This method supplements natural groundwater recharge by either injecting or infiltrating water into the ground. Various techniques are employed in MAR, including the use of infiltration ponds, injection wells, and riverbank filtration. Groundwater depletion is a significant issue in the Barind area, where the rate of decline ranges from 0.75 to 1.25 feet per year. This is exacerbated by limited natural aquifer recharge and high irrigation demands, leading to the ineffectiveness of some suction pumps. To address depletion, two primary strategies are suggested: Utilizing groundwater within safe yield limits, which requires considerable time for aquifer recovery, and enhancing groundwater recharge through artificial recharge mechanisms. Artificial recharge also offers additional benefits, such as mitigating salinity issues in coastal areas and managing water storage in urban centers like Dhaka. However, the disadvantages of MAR projects should also be taken into consideration before implementation. Implementing a MAR project necessitates a conceptual understanding of aquifer characteristics, such as the presence and type of top aquitard (clay or silt), aquitard and aquifer thickness, hydraulic conductivity, transmissivity, and specific yield. Properly designing a recharge well and assigning a recharge rate is critical; designing pumping and recharge wells involve different considerations. A low recharge rate is safer but prolongs the aquifer's recharge time, while a high rate risks clogging the aquifer, which occurs when pores are blocked, preventing adequate water flow if the rate exceeds hydraulic conductivity. Therefore, careful site specific design of recharge rates and well spacing is essential. The success of a MAR project fully depends on appropriate site specific design of the project. Water quality is also a significant concern, particularly if contaminated water is used, as it can detrimentally damage aquifers. The preferred water sources rank as follows: 1) rainwater (low contaminated), 2) pond and lake water (moderately contaminated), and 3) river water, which in Bangladesh is compromised by urban pollution. Studies indicate river water quality varies from fair to marginal, with high levels of sulphate and contamination risks like arsenic and salinity. Thus, river water must be treated to remove contaminants before it can be safely injected into the aquifer. Dr. Mohammad Abul Fazal is a specialist in agricultural engineering. He achieved his PhD in groundwater management from Kyoto University, Japan.

The United Nations General Assembly voted on Friday to renew Volker Turk’s mandate as high commissioner for human rights for four years despite strong opposition from the United States, Russia and Israel.

By a vote of 144 in favour, 10 against, and 13 abstentions, the assembly approved the renewal, beginning October 12, 2026, as proposed by UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres.

An alternative proposal from Russia to extend the mandate by only a few months, until December 31, 2026, was overwhelmingly rejected, as was the US request to postpone the vote.

Ambassador Jeff Bartos, US representative for UN management and reform, criticised the four-year renewal on both procedural and substantive grounds, accusing Guterres of having rushed the process.

“Make no mistake: If this assembly tolerates procedural overreach, backroom deals, and the misuse of UN posts, there will be consequences.

“The United States will immediately reassess our engagement, participation, and funding,” he warned just before the vote, accusing Guterres of having rushed the timetable “to hand his long-term friend a four-year executive payout”.

French Ambassador Jerome Bonnafont, however, described Turk as “a voice of conscience” who had demonstrated “rigour and impartiality” during his first term.

Turk, an Austrian jurist, has served as high commissioner since October 2022. He has emphasised the universality of human rights and the need to apply international law equally.

During his tenure, he has been outspoken on the Russian invasion of Ukraine, the war in Gaza, Afghanistan, Sudan, Bangladesh, Myanmar and Nicaragua.

But he’s also been criticised for not taking more decisive positions on Cuba, the plight of Uyghurs in Xinjiang, China, and for not directly using the word “genocide” in reference to Gaza, unlike several UN experts and rapporteurs.

Turk’s stances have earned him sharp criticism from several governments, notably Russia and Israel.

Both nations’ ambassadors voiced opposition Friday to his renewal, saying Guterres, whose term as secretary-general expires at the end of the year, should have left the selection of the human rights commissioner to his successor.

item.title: Does the government have a concrete plan for child safety?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, GPT-OSS-120B

Last month, in my opinion article, “ Child Safety: Beyond Ideological Polarization ,” published in the Dhaka Tribune, I argued that the sexual abuse of children -- including cases occurring within madrasa settings -- is fundamentally a structural governance challenge rooted in weak accountability mechanisms, regulatory failures, and institutional neglect. The urgency of this argument has become even more evident in recent days. Disturbing content has been circulating on TikTok, featuring madrasa teachers openly sexualizing and objectifying their child students. Accompanied by provocative comments, this trend reveals a deeper social crisis: The normalization of predatory attitudes toward children and the total absence of effective preventive safeguards. It forces us to confront an uncomfortable question: Why do these educational institutions continue to fail to ensure child safety, and why does the state allow it? To answer these questions, we must look beyond surface-level moral failings and examine the institutional architecture within which these abuses occur. Bangladesh’s response to child protection crises remains trapped in a reactive cycle. After every tragedy, public anger intensifies, demands for justice peak, and political leaders offer swift sympathy. Following the heartbreaking Ramisa case, the prime minister’s visit to the victim's family and commitment to justice provided necessary, immediate reassurance. Such gestures matter, but they cannot substitute for the institutional systems required to prevent abuse before it occurs. Before the election, the prime minister repeatedly assured the public, " I have a plan ” for the nation. We must now ask for the procedural details of the plan regarding the protection of children. We can no longer afford institutional silence, nor can we accept abstract promises. The current crisis demands a coordinated national response. The government should initiate immediate cross-sector collaboration to develop a concrete, actionable child protection roadmap. This roadmap cannot remain a policy document alone; it must address the deep, internal layers of madrasa management -- including labour standards, teacher residency rules, child protection training, independent monitoring, complaint mechanisms, and external oversight. Most importantly, the roadmap must answer practical questions: How will children be protected tomorrow? How will the educational institutions be monitored? What mechanisms will ensure absolute accountability? A plan on paper is not a plan in practice. The true measure of leadership is not how effectively it responds to public outrage after harm occurs, but whether it builds institutions capable of preventing abuse in the first place. Our children deserve more than sympathy after they suffer; they deserve a system designed to protect them before tragedy strikes. Aisha Siddika is a PhD Candidate at McMaster University, Canada. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s directive to swiftly rehabilitate hawkers evicted from Dhaka’s streets is a necessary intervention in a problem that has dragged on for far too long. Hawkers are not criminals but workers, and a key part of our informal economy. When they are evicted without a plan, the consequences are immediate and severe. Creating a situation where they struggle to earn, or are forced to operate in unsafe or unsuitable locations, or pushed into debt, is not a solution. The PM’s words must therefore be treated as a directive to rethink how Dhaka handles its informal workforce. Hawkers need designated, well‑planned vending zones, not ad‑hoc spaces that shift with every police operation. They need clear rules, not arbitrary enforcement along with basic facilities so that their workplaces are dignified and safe. item.title: Saving our tigers. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:

The revelation that Bangladesh has only 189 tigers left should be treated for what it is - a national tragedy. The Royal Bengal Tiger is the most iconic species we have as a nation, it is quite literally the symbol of our natural heritage. That its numbers keep dwindling, and State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salauddin warning that the current situation is not sufficient to protect the species from extinction, is deeply concerning. When tiger numbers continue to fall, it signals deeper ecological distress that cannot be ignored. Experts have long cautioned that habitat loss, rising salinity, human encroachment, poaching, and climate‑driven changes in the Sundarbans are eroding the conditions tigers need to survive. The latest numbers only confirm that these pressures are intensifying. Conserving tigers should not be viewed as only about protecting a single species. It is about safeguarding the entire biodiversity of the Sundarbans - our most critical natural buffer against natural disasters such as cyclones and tidal surges. Bangladesh has taken steps: Strengthening patrols, expanding camera‑trap monitoring, and improving community engagement. However, it is plain to see that the scale of the challenge demands more. Conservation must be backed by sustained investment, scientific research, and strict enforcement against poaching and illegal resource extraction. The forest also needs better protection from industrial pressures, unregulated tourism, and climate impacts that are already reshaping its landscape. We must also broaden our focus beyond tigers. Biodiversity loss has been accelerating nationwide, from wetlands to hill forests to coastal ecosystems. Protecting wildlife therefore requires a holistic strategy, from restoring habitats to regulating development to integrating conservation into national planning rather than treating it as an isolated sector. The tiger population can recover, but only if we are able to act decisively, consistently, and with long‑term vision. Saving the tiger means saving the Sundarbans, and saving the Sundarbans means protecting our future.

Today is World Day Against Trafficking in Persons, and is a reminder that human trafficking remains one of the most persistent and damaging crimes. Every year, thousands of Bangladeshis fall victim to traffickers. Yet, trafficking is no longer confined to borders, brokers, or physical coercion. Much of it has moved online, and we are now facing a new generation of threats that exploit digital technology, social media, and the vulnerabilities of young people seeking opportunity. Human trafficking has always preyed on desperation. Today, it also preys on connectivity. Recruiters no longer need to visit villages or operate through local agents; they can reach victims through Facebook groups, messaging apps, job portals, and livestream platforms. From false job offers to fraudulent migration schemes, the digital shift has made trafficking faster, harder to detect, and easier to disguise as legitimate opportunity. For Bangladesh, this evolution is especially dangerous. Millions of young people are online, often without digital literacy or awareness of the risks. Migrant workers increasingly rely on social media for job information. Traffickers have adapted, and our protection systems must adapt with equal speed. Bangladesh has made progress in combating traditional trafficking routes, strengthening laws, and improving rescue and rehabilitation. But the digital dimension remains under-addressed. Law enforcement lacks specialized cyber‑trafficking units. Border and migration officials are not always trained to identify victims recruited online. And survivors often struggle to navigate the legal system when exploitation begins on a screen rather than at a border. On this day, the message is clear: Strengthening protection means also strengthening digital vigilance. Traffickers are online and Bangladesh must be ready to meet them there. Trafficking has changed and our response must change with it. We cannot rely on old tools to fight a new threat.

item.title: When childhood becomes the first casualty of climate change. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
[Priority]

Systemic Significance

Selected by: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Llama-3.3-70B, GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20

There was a time when climate change in Bangladesh was discussed through the language of infrastructure. The conversation revolved around embankments, cyclone shelters, flood control projects, adaptation funds, and carbon emissions. Success was measured by the number of kilometres of embankments built or the amount of international climate finance secured. Children appeared in these discussions only as passive victims to be rescued after disaster struck. The latest Children’s Climate Risk Report 2026 by Unicef demands that we abandon that habit of thinking. It suggests something far more unsettling. Bangladesh is not merely fighting a climate crisis. It is slowly becoming a place where childhood itself is being reshaped by an environment that is growing increasingly hostile. This is perhaps the most important lesson hidden beneath the report’s alarming statistics. Climate change is no longer only about damaged roads, submerged villages or destroyed crops. It is altering what it means to grow up in Bangladesh. The report places Bangladesh fourth among the countries where children face the highest climate risks, with an overall vulnerability score of 9.38 out of 10. Only Myanmar, Pakistan, and Vietnam rank higher. Bangladesh receives the maximum possible risk score, 10 out of 10, for riverine flooding, making its children the most exposed in the world to this particular hazard. The country’s scores remain alarmingly high across nearly every category, including tropical cyclones at 9.7, air pollution at 9.7, drought at 9.65, extreme heat at 9.24, and coastal flooding at 8.13. These numbers are disturbing enough. Yet the real story lies in what they collectively reveal. Climate disasters rarely arrive one at a time anymore. Bangladesh increasingly experiences overlapping emergencies where one hazard begins before another has fully disappeared. Floods are followed by disease outbreaks. Cyclones are followed by prolonged displacement. Heatwaves arrive before communities recover from previous disasters. Air pollution quietly intensifies throughout the year, affecting children even when skies appear clear. The report captures this reality by arguing that Bangladeshi children are exposed not to isolated disasters but to multiple climate shocks simultaneously. Nearly 60 million children in Bangladesh are exposed to at least one climate-related hazard. More than 24 million face the combined risks of floods, droughts, and cyclones. Around 32 million children are directly threatened by riverine flooding, about 22 million by cyclones, while roughly 60 million are exposed to drought and air pollution. These figures are difficult to comprehend because they describe an entire generation rather than isolated communities. The tendency is often to think of climate change through dramatic images of flooded villages or collapsing riverbanks. Those images matter, but they obscure a slower crisis unfolding inside classrooms, hospitals, and homes. When schools become shelters after cyclones, education stops. When repeated flooding destroys family income, children become workers instead of students. When prolonged displacement breaks community networks, girls become more vulnerable to early marriage while boys face greater pressure to enter informal labour markets. Health deteriorates because clean drinking water becomes scarce, sanitation systems collapse and disease spreads more easily. The damage extends well beyond the immediate disaster. A child who misses several months of education today may experience lower earnings decades later. A malnourished infant exposed to repeated climate shocks may never fully recover physically or cognitively. Psychological trauma caused by repeated disasters often remains invisible, although it shapes behaviour and emotional well-being for years. These are losses that no disaster compensation package can fully repair. One of the most overlooked findings in the Unicef report is that Bangladesh actually performs comparatively better in several traditional child development indicators such as child health, nutrition, education, poverty reduction, and maternal mortality. In other words, the country has made genuine progress over the past decades. Yet climate change threatens to reverse those achievements. The environmental conditions necessary to sustain these gains are becoming increasingly unstable. Development successes built over decades now stand on uncertain ecological foundations. Perhaps this explains why conventional adaptation strategies increasingly appear insufficient. Much of Bangladesh’s climate planning understandably focuses on physical infrastructure. Cyclone shelters save lives. Embankments reduce flood damage. River dredging improves water management. These remain essential investments. However, the next stage of adaptation requires a different question. Instead of asking how infrastructure survives climate change, policy-makers must ask how childhood survives climate change. These are not identical questions. Children experience disasters differently from adults because their bodies, minds, and futures are still developing. A week without school affects an eight-year-old differently than it affects a thirty-year-old office worker. Air pollution permanently damages developing lungs more severely than adult lungs. Malnutrition during childhood produces lifelong consequences that cannot simply be reversed later. The report estimates that around 337 million children worldwide face riverine flooding, 662 million face tropical storms, 33 million are exposed to coastal flooding, approximately 1.2 billion experience extreme heat and nearly 1.8 billion face drought. Around 80% of children exposed to riverine and coastal flooding live in only 10 countries, with Bangladesh among the most heavily affected. These global figures remind us that Bangladesh occupies the frontline of a worldwide crisis. Yet unlike wealthier nations, Bangladesh must confront this emergency while still addressing poverty, rapid urbanization, infrastructure deficits, and demographic pressures. This makes policy choices especially important. Climate adaptation cannot remain concentrated only within environment ministries. It must become the organizing principle across education, public health, urban planning, and social protection. A single national blueprint cannot adequately protect them all. Floating schools may be appropriate in flood-prone wetlands. Residential educational facilities may prove more effective in remote hill regions. Coastal districts require stronger shelter systems designed specifically around children’s needs. Urban schools increasingly need shaded environments capable of protecting students during prolonged heatwaves. Climate adaptation succeeds only when geography shapes policy. Equally important is recognizing that children are not merely recipients of protection. Young people increasingly understand climate risks because they experience them firsthand. Many already participate in community preparedness programs, environmental campaigns, and local adaptation initiatives. Their perspectives often reveal practical problems adults overlook. Treating children solely as vulnerable populations ignores their potential as active participants in building resilience. Unicef rightly argues that children should be meaningfully included in climate policy-making. This is not symbolic participation. It reflects the reality that today’s policy decisions will define their entire futures far more than they will affect current decision-makers. There is also an uncomfortable issue the international community cannot continue avoiding. Bangladeshi children contribute almost nothing to global greenhouse gas emissions. Yet they bear some of the world’s highest climate risks. This remains one of the greatest moral failures of modern international politics. The countries and populations least responsible for warming the planet continue paying its highest human costs. Climate justice therefore cannot remain confined to abstract diplomatic language during international summits. It must translate into predictable adaptation finance, technology transfer, and long-term investments focused specifically on children’s well-being. HM Nazmul Alam is an Academic, Journalist, and Political Analyst based in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Currently he teaches at IUBAT.
